To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) an exogenous increase in foreign debt inflows leads, after about two years, to an increase in GDP, stock prices, inflation and credit growth, and an appreciation of real exchange rate; (2) an exogenous decrease in foreign debt inflow leads, after about a year, to a decrease in GDP, stock price, inflation and credit, and a depreciation of the real exchange rate; and (3) an exogenous change in foreign equity inflows has no significant effect

(i) the macroeconomic effects are almost entirely due, in our sample, to debt inflows, not equity inflows; (ii) debt inflows are associated with higher GDP growth, inflation, stock market prices, credit growth and an appreciating real exchange rate, and (iii) equity inflows are not associated with any significant macroeconomic effects in our sample.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether capital inflows have the same macroeconomic effects, regardless of the source of the capital inflow.
the macroeconomic consequences of debt- and equitybased capital inflows.
whether debt- and-equity-based capital inflows are different in their macroeconomic effects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the macroeconomic effects are almost entirely due not to capital inflows but to the composition of capital inflows.

equity-based capital inflow has almost no effect and debt-based capital inflow leads to a significant appreciation of the exchange rates, an increase in inflation, an increase in stock prices, and a rise in credit growth, which in turn leads to an increase in the output.
the effects on the macroeconomy of capital inflows are not due to the fact that capital inflows are either debt or equity-based, but to the fact that they are debt-based.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
debt-based capital inflows are expansionary and equity-based capital are not.
the macroeconomic effects are driven by the debt component of capital inflow.
the macroeconomic effects are almost entirely due not to the amount of capital inflows, but to the composition of capital inflows.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the macroeconomic effects are not driven by the composition of the inflows but by the total inflows.

the macroeconomic effects associated with the capital inflows experienced by emerging market countries are almost entirely the result of the debt component of those inflows, and that these effects are quite similar to those associated with the debt inflows of earlier decades.
the macroeconomic effects associated with a given increase in capital inflows are not driven by the composition of capital inflows, but rather by the level of capital inflows.
